stem: Why must an organization's digital accessibility evaluation strategy combine automated testing tools with human manual testing?

options.text: Because automated scanners evaluate subjective cognitive readability and plain language, whereas manual testers validate DOM syntax rules.
options.shortLabel: Scanners test readability; humans test syntax
options.rationale: This inverts reality: automated tools are adept at verifying algorithmic DOM syntax and machine-checkable rules, whereas human evaluators are required to assess subjective qualities like plain language, cognitive flow, and context.

options.text: Because automated scanners detect only a subset of barriers and cannot evaluate contextual meaning, logical flow, or usability.
options.shortLabel: Scanners catch partial issues; humans assess context
options.rationale: Automated testing catches roughly 30–40% of potential barriers (such as missing attributes and color contrast formulas), but human evaluation is essential to judge contextual meaning, keyboard navigation, and actual screen reader usability.

options.text: Because international accessibility standards mandate manual testing documentation to grant formal statutory immunity from regulatory enforcement investigations.
options.rationale: While manual testing is essential for comprehensive quality, neither WCAG nor international civil rights laws grant statutory immunity or legal safe harbors based on manual evaluation logs.

options.text: Because automated evaluation engines cannot execute client-side JavaScript, rendering them unable to audit modern single-page web applications.
options.rationale: Modern automated tools (such as Axe-core and Lighthouse) run directly inside browser rendering engines and readily parse client-side JavaScript; their limitation is human judgment, not script execution.

explanation: A complete digital accessibility evaluation strategy requires both automated and manual testing. Automated testing tools provide speed and scale, catching syntax errors, missing attributes, and programmatic issues across thousands of pages. However, automated scanners can only detect an estimated 30% to 40% of WCAG success criteria. They cannot determine whether alternative text is meaningful in context, whether keyboard focus follows a logical sequence, or whether complex dynamic widgets are truly usable with assistive technology like screen readers. Human manual testing bridges this critical gap.
